title: Knee Replacement Recovery Timeline: What to Expect, Stage by Stage
seo_title: Knee Replacement Recovery Timeline | Elite Sports Medicine
description: What knee replacement recovery looks like from the day of surgery to six months, what not to do, when you can drive or work, and when to call.
body_html:
Most people go into a knee replacement focused on the operation. The part that decides how the knee feels a year later is the recovery that follows it. Knowing roughly what each stage looks like makes it easier to plan time off, arrange help at home and tell a normal bad day from a problem. Here is what to expect, stage by stage, and what to avoid along the way.

Every recovery is different. Your surgeon’s instructions for your knee always come first, and the timings below are general ranges, not deadlines.

What does the recovery timeline look like at a glance?

StageWhat it usually involves
Day of surgeryStanding and walking with support, such as a walker
First two weeksSwelling and soreness, short walks, exercises to bend and straighten the knee, wound care
Weeks 3 to 6Moving away from the walker, longer walks, more of daily life back
Weeks 6 to 12Where the meaningful gains in comfort and function usually show up
Up to six months and beyondStrength, stamina and range of motion keep improving

What happens on the day of knee replacement surgery?

You will be up sooner than you might expect. Most people are up and walking with support, such as a walker, on the day of surgery. That first walk is short, but it is the start of the rehabilitation that decides the result.

Pain is managed with a combination of medicines, and sometimes a nerve block placed around the time of surgery. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) advises using opioids only as directed and stopping them as soon as the pain begins to ease. Whether you go home the same day or stay overnight depends on your health and the plan your surgeon sets with you.

What should I expect in the first two weeks after knee replacement?

This is usually the hardest stretch. The knee is swollen, stiff and sore, sleep is broken, and some people lose their appetite for a while. None of that means something has gone wrong. Pain with activity and at night is common for several weeks after surgery, according to the AAOS.

The work in these two weeks is simple but repetitive:

  • Walking a little, several times a day, and a little further each day
  • Doing the exercises your therapist gives you to bend and straighten the knee
  • Elevating the leg and using ice when the knee swells or aches after exercise
  • Keeping the wound clean and dry, and not soaking it until it has fully sealed
  • Taking any blood clot prevention measures your surgeon prescribes

The AAOS calls exercise a critical part of home care, particularly in the first few weeks. Getting the knee to straighten fully and bend a little further each week is the main goal early on.

When do most people feel better after a knee replacement?

Somewhere between weeks three and six, most people notice a turn. The AAOS says you should be able to resume most normal activities of daily living within 3 to 6 weeks of surgery. The walker gives way to a cane or nothing at all, walks get longer, and getting in and out of a chair or a car stops being an event.

The meaningful gains usually come over the six to twelve weeks after surgery. That is the window in which therapy pays off most, so it is worth protecting: keep the appointments and do the home exercises on the days you do not feel like it. Strength, stamina and range of motion keep improving after that, and full recovery can take up to six months.

A few things surprise people. Most notice some numbness in the skin around the incision, some stiffness with deep bending, and a little clicking when the knee bends or they walk. The AAOS describes these as normal, and they often become less noticeable with time.

What should you not do after a knee replacement?

Most setbacks come from doing too little or too much too soon. The common ones to avoid:

  • Skipping the exercises. A knee that is rested instead of moved tends to stiffen. The exercises are the treatment, not an extra.
  • Overdoing a good day. A long walk on day ten can mean a swollen, painful day eleven. Build up steadily.
  • Leaving trip hazards at home. Loose rugs, cords and clutter are a real risk while you are on a walker, and the AAOS warns that a fall in the first few weeks can damage a new knee.
  • Driving before you are cleared. More on that below.
  • Returning to high-impact activity on your own schedule. Running and jumping sports are a conversation to have with your surgeon, not a decision to make once the knee feels good.

How can I make the recovery easier before surgery?

A little preparation removes a lot of stress in the first weeks. The AAOS recommends arranging for someone to help at home for the first several days to several weeks, moving the things you use most within easy reach, clearing walkways for a walker, and, if you can, setting up a firm chair with a higher seat, a shower chair and a raised toilet seat. If your bedroom is upstairs, a temporary bed on the ground floor can make the first week much easier.

It also helps to bring a list of questions to your pre-operative visit: how long you will need the walker, when therapy starts and where, and what your restrictions will be.

When can I drive, go back to work and play golf again?

Driving. Only once you are off sedating pain medication and can control the car safely. That depends on which knee was replaced and whether your car is automatic or manual. Dr. Matarazzo clears patients at a follow-up visit rather than by a fixed calendar date.

Work. It depends on what your job asks of you. Desk-based work is often resumed far sooner than physical or on-your-feet work. You will get a realistic range for your own job at your pre-operative visit, and the office can provide documentation for your employer.

Golf and other activities. Low-impact activity, such as walking, cycling and golf, is expected after rehabilitation. When you return to each one is decided as your strength and motion come back.

What warning signs mean I should call the office?

Some swelling, warmth and soreness are normal. These are not, and the AAOS lists them as reasons to contact your doctor promptly:

  • Increasing pain, tenderness or swelling in the calf, ankle or foot, which can be a sign of a blood clot
  • A persistent fever or chills, increasing redness, tenderness or swelling around the wound, drainage from it, or knee pain that keeps increasing at rest and with activity, which can be signs of infection
  • Sudden shortness of breath or chest pain, which needs emergency care right away

Does a partial or MAKO knee replacement change the recovery?

It can. A partial knee replacement resurfaces only the worn compartment, so recovery is usually quicker than after a total. Fewer people qualify for one, because most arthritic knees have wear in more than one area. The partial vs. total comparison covers who is a candidate.

With MAKO robotic-arm assisted knee replacement, the operation is planned in 3D from a CT scan of your own knee, and the arm holds the surgeon to that plan. Less disruption to the surrounding tissue can show up in the early recovery. The rehabilitation still has to be done, though. Whatever the technique, a structured rehabilitation plan is what decides the result.

Dr. Marc F. Matarazzo is a board-certified, fellowship-trained orthopedic surgeon, certified in the MAKO system, and performs total and partial knee replacements for patients in Port St. Lucie and Palm Beach Gardens.

Not sure you are ready for a replacement?

Not every painful knee needs one. Knee arthritis treatment covers the full range, from therapy and injections to the MISHA Knee System. If a replacement is the right answer, total knee replacement explains what the operation involves.
